📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The act of gift-giving always seems incredibly fun before the holidays come around. But I doubt I’m the only one who has suddenly come to in a sweaty, consumerist panic after all the presents are unwrapped and there is wrapping paper and ribbon on the floor, wishing I’d put my money somewhere meaningful instead of showering my little cousins with books they are exceedingly polite about but clearly hate.

That’s why, in recent years, I’ve made the decision to donate to an important cause in a loved one’s name—and I’ve never, ever regretted it. Below, find a roundup of some of the Vogue staff’s favorite organizations doing hard and necessary work that could use a little love this holiday season:.

According to recent reports, “I always give to the Red Cross in the wake of natural disasters, but this year the cause was a little closer to home when the organization stepped in to provide relief to those displaced by the terrible building collapse that took place in Flatbush earlier this month. I live near the building site, and for several nights, the entire neighborhood was kept awake by hovering helicopters, a terrible reminder of the tragedy that had occurred. There have been many initiatives since, organized by friends and neighbors, to provide assistance. But for those who might like to bolster the resilient spirit of Latest York City this holiday season from farther afield, a donation to the Red Cross would be worthwhile.” —Chloe Schama.

“As someone who has always loved reading, I believe books have the power to open up new worlds, spark our imaginations, and inspire us to dream bigger. Every child deserves the opportunity to experience that same magic. Behind the Book brings diverse books and authors into underserved New York City public school classrooms, helping children discover the joy of reading and storytelling.” —Molly Barstein.

According to recent reports, one person is diagnosed with cancer every 1.6 seconds worldwide, and the Breakthrough Board is a women’s coalition that has been funding life-saving cancer research at the University of Chicago for nearly 80 years. Vogue Senior Digital Line Editor Jane Chun recommends donating and/or volunteering your time for this worthy cause.

Many of us would be at a loss without our furry companions, so a donation to this animal welfare organization—which operates the largest no-kill animal shelter in the US in Kanab, Utah, and partners with shelters and rescue groups nationwide—is a particularly nice way to honor the beloved pet in your life.

United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has detained over 8,000 children and increased family separations under the Trump administration. A donation to this California-based nonprofit (which will be matched through the end of December) helps to support those children and families with critical legal resources, medical and psychological treatment, and other forms of sorely needed support.

This nonprofit organization, which will have Vogue Head of Editorial Content Chloe Malle’s support this year, has been helping people affected by conflict and disaster around the world for the past 90 years. It is currently matching donations for families in Gaza (times three) through Giving Tuesday.

Over 10 million older adults live in poverty in the US, and this organization—which was founded by a Philadelphia social worker in 1954—works to mitigate that sad state of affairs by delivering healthy, culturally sensitive meals (and needed social contact) to seniors around the country.

It has been revealed that A donation to this organization attempting to find a cure for multiple myeloma (a type of blood cancer that forms in plasma cells) goes particularly far right now, notes Vogue Fashion Commerce Director Madeline Fass, as every dollar you give before December 31 will be doubled—up to $1 million—thanks to a special matching challenge from Dr. Elsey’s Fund to Cure Cancer.

With ICE raids and arrests ongoing all over the country, a donation to the Los Angeles-based National Day Laborer Organizing Network’s Immigrant Defense Fund helps to support legal defense and public advocacy for immigrant communities under attack.

Industry observers note that the right to a safe, accessible abortion has only become more imperiled since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, and this nonprofit network of over 100 independent, grassroots abortion funds is working to increase access and make sure no pregnant person is forced to go without potentially lifesaving care.

Federal funding for NPR, PBS, and local public media stations was ended by President Donald Trump in 2025, but you can step up and help fill the gap by donating directly to your local station to support independent journalism. “I initiative to support my local NPR station, WNYC,” says Chloe Malle.

Nobody should be forced to navigate the aftermath of sexual assault or misconduct alone, and a donation to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN) helps fund vital services like the organization’s national 24-hour sexual assault hotline to ensure that survivors always have somewhere to turn.

In a recent development, there are tons of great organizations working to end hunger in the US, from Feeding America to Feed the Children, but sometimes it’s nice to find one working locally. For Fresh Yorkers, that might just be this Harlem-based nonprofit that serves 900 free, chef-prepared meals a week to community members facing hunger.

It’s a scary time for trans, nonbinary, and gender-nonconforming youth in the US, which makes a donation to this mutual aid project serving unhoused and/or vulnerable trans youth (or a gift purchased directly from someone’s registry) particularly meaningful.

“I plan to adopt a couple of snowy owls for the children in my life through the World Wildlife Fund,” notes Malle—and you, too, can help prevent the vulnerable species’s extinction (while nabbing yourself a snowy owl plush toy) by donating to the WWF.

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

Industry observers note that alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being promptly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. The brine from the canned artichoke hearts allows the feta to melt down in the oven, which in turn coats the artichoke hearts, creating a velvety dip. The best part about this recipe is that it’s completely customizable. My favorite variation includes adding honey, thyme, and an olive topper, which elevates the dip to a whole new level. Serve it with crunchy crostini or pita chips at your next dinner party, and your guests will go crazy.

Breaking: Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work.
  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.
  • Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our newly introduced app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

Sources indicate that with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

In a recent development, every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

It has been revealed that there is a newly introduced vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

It has been revealed that with a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

According to recent reports, my Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

We have a newly introduced Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

Industry observers note that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that former Maine Gov.
  • Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once noted he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once noted he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Industry observers note that dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

According to recent reports, “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

It has been revealed that lePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent Latest England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Recent findings suggest that golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

In a recent development, “I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially introduced his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, promptly empty the contents into a newly introduced pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Recent findings suggest that scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

It has been revealed that if you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

According to recent reports, the Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

It has been revealed that mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Recent findings suggest that using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

Sources indicate that according to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up latest recipes.

In a recent development, since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

#135784. Tech Report: The Secondhand Gifting Conundrum

Tech Report: The Secondhand Gifting Conundrum

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Asking for a friend: would you be happy with a secondhand gift for Christmas?
  • Recent findings suggest that in the current holiday preamble, shoppers are seeking out pre-loved luxury, and hopeful recipients are adding resale finds to their wishlists.
  • According to Rati Sahi Levesque, The RealReal CEO, gift shoppers are spending big and small this holiday season: designer accessories under $250 and collectible pieces over $10,000.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Asking for a friend: would you be happy with a secondhand gift for Christmas?

Recent findings suggest that in the current holiday preamble, shoppers are seeking out pre-loved luxury, and hopeful recipients are adding resale finds to their wishlists. While aspirational consumers seek more bang for their buck, top-end consumers favor one-of-a-kind pieces with a story to tell.

According to Rati Sahi Levesque, The RealReal CEO, gift shoppers are spending big and small this holiday season: designer accessories under $250 and collectible pieces over $10,000. “One of the things I love about resale is that great taste isn’t confined to a particular price point,” she notes, explaining that shoppers can do more with less, or invest in something extraordinary for their recipient. “Resale gives you access to things that money alone can’t buy in the primary market.”.

Recent findings suggest that this November, Vinted searches for Christmas gifts were up 35% year on year, with interest building steadily since August, according to the platform. Similarly, on Depop, searches for “Christmas gifts” grew 248% year on year, climbing another 321% in the last month. The small luxuries category is building momentum for gifting, with searches for “Coachtopia” and “tall Uggs” up 132% and 96%, respectively, in the last month.

Sources indicate that according to Deloitte’s holiday shopping report, 29% of US consumers may buy pre-owned luxury items as Christmas gifts this year. In the UK, 47% of 18 to 45-year-olds are willing to gift pre-loved items, per Ebay’s recent re-commerce report.

The RealReal Holiday campaign 2026.

In a recent development, the pre-loved gifting surge is in line with broader growth in resale. In 2025, Boston Consulting Group and Vestiaire Collective estimated the global secondhand market’s value at $210-220 billion, forecasting a value of $320-$360 billion by 2030. As mentioned, value for money is a substantial draw, against a backdrop of inflation and a cost-of-living crisis. Vinted reports that the average adult fashion item sold on the platform is 72% less than RRP, while 69% of members believe Vinted gives them access to higher-quality or designer brands. For some shoppers, it’s also a way to resist the consumerism and waste associated with Christmas.

In this landscape, and as Gen Zs continue to favor messier, more eclectic and unique styling, gifting vintage is no longer niche. Nor is it easy. For gift-givers, pre-loved presents often involve more mental labor — either for the customer or their personal shopper. It requires skill to source a rarefied handbag or archival design — especially one in good condition.

As well as middle-income shoppers, high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) are shopping secondhand this Christmas, with higher-ticket spending on rarefied goods. Sarah Jordan Buss, founder of The Vintage Project, a Beverly Hills boutique esteemed for high-profile clients, states that the budget for gifting usually sits around $1,000. Paris-founded resale platform Resee is also popular with HNWIs at Christmas. “The holiday gifting season is huge for us,” says co-founder and CEO Sofia Bernardin.

Industry observers note that the rub? If shoppers are to nail that choice, platforms and sellers need to demonstrate that the gift has provenance, quality, authenticity and a story behind it. Competitors fighting for market share must sharpen their value proposition through personalization, product curation, clienteling, and strong certification measures.

According to recent reports, for wealthy gifters, the process before the transaction is important. Evangeline Li is a high-net-worth curator based in London who often shops vintage accessories and jewelry to gift. She looks to 1990s Chanel, vintage Trifari and Mikimoto designs. Her spend bracket per gift is around £300-£1,000, depending on the person and piece. “I enjoy the hunt almost as much as the discovery itself,” she says, adding that she regularly visits antique markets in Britain, flea markets in Paris, and vintage stores in Japan, while also trawling Ebay, Etsy and Google.

Platforms report a strong interest in secondary market Chanel for Christmas gifting.

More recently, Li has become increasingly reliant on AI in her sourcing process. “It’s particularly useful when I’m searching for something unusual or difficult to describe as it can lead me to objects, designers and specialist dealers I might not otherwise have discovered,” she says.

In a recent development, for Li, it’s not just about designer names, but the historic and sentimental value. “I also enjoy finding gifts that are a little unexpected or playful: antique dice for friends who love games, a mid-century Tiffany & Co. double-deck playing card set in its signature blue box, or nostalgic collectibles such as Pokémon cards and vintage Hello Kitty dolls,” she claims.

The RealReal’s Levesque concurs. “It doesn't have to be a substantial, recognizable logo. A vintage gold pendant for someone who loves layering jewelry or a beautiful Loro Piana belt for someone with a very understated wardrobe can feel much more personal than the obvious choice.” As she sees it, for affluent loved ones, the most desirable fashion items are pieces you can’t buy firsthand — they’re gifts the recipient might never have discovered.

When Buss is advising a client on a vintage gift, she has a few techniques to make it extra special. Often, she pulls a design from the year the intended recipient was born. “People really respond to that detail,” she states. Another technique is to consider small anecdotes the recipient might have made. “It might be a collection they mentioned in passing months ago or a piece from a designer they’ve loved for years — even something they regret getting rid of,” she says.

Resee also records an appetite for highly personalized luxury gifts. On the platform, the famous “Love” poster cards that Yves Saint Laurent would send to his collaborators annually have become a go-to gift during the holidays. Because they are dated — the series ran between 1970 and 2007 — gift givers choose specific designs with the same date as the recipient’s birth year. “It’s all about giving people something that feels as though it was specifically found for them,” states Bernardin. Of course, online, fakes and copies of these posters are rife, but Resee’s authentic poster cards come with the original postage stamps and shipping tubes, which offer a culturally richer gift. “I think the storytelling aspect is so important when it comes to giving a vintage gift,” Bernardin adds.

The RealReal’s holiday gifting guide.

For Buss, bags are the most common gift clients request, and Chanel, Gucci and Chloé are some of the most popular brands. Often, the founder tells Vogue Business, she receives client requests for the original versions of bags that have been reissued, such as Saint Laurent’s Mombasa design and the Chloé Paddington, signaling the importance of provenance and cultural cachet. Secondhand marketplace 1stDibs is seeing traction on items such as Elsa Peretti’s Tiffany & Co. designs, Cartier watches, Hermès scarves, and iconic handbags and travel bags. Hard-to-find releases, such as Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel designs also perform well for gifting. “Buyers are gravitating toward classics that are easy to gift and easy to style, and that the recipient will cherish for years,” claims Anthony Barzilay Freund, 1stDibs’s editorial director and director of fine art.

Industry observers note that on The RealReal, consumers continue to spend healthily on household names: Hermès, Prada, Gucci, Cartier, Rolex and Tiffany & Co. “But what I find equally interesting is the appetite for pieces that are a little less expected,” says Levesque, pointing to momentum in emerging designers and distinctive finds — whether that’s a statement sweater from Zankov or collectible ornaments by artist Caroline Zimbalist. The executive also points to strong demand for archival pieces tied to specific designer eras, such as an Yves Saint Laurent Rive Gauche tassel belt from the 1970s or an embellished Chloé bag from the Phoebe Philo era.

Recent findings suggest that ebay also observes an interest in archival gifting. Kirsty Keoghan, Ebay’s general manager for fashion and luxury in Europe, highlights Prada’s sportier line, Linea Rossa, debuted in 1997, as well as Pucci and Blumarine as significant hits. She also calls out Karl Lagerfeld-era Chanel, John Galliano’s Dior and Tom Ford-era Gucci.

Industry observers note that “Vintage is not a renewable resource and is thus the ultimate luxury,” states Mattie Barringer, co-founder of cult fashion and art label Women’s History Museum, which also runs a vintage boutique within the brand’s Canal Street store. The boutique’s esoteric range specializes in collectible items with fashion-historical value, spanning ’20s pumps through to ’90s Jean Paul Gaultier tops, as well as a selection of items under $100 for smaller budgets. “We feel an item or object with a life before really connects us to our shared humanity and history. What could be more Christmassy!”.

Sources indicate that while pre-loved gifting is gaining traction, shoppers can be put off by a few obstacles. Many of them are the same hangups associated with vintage in general. Where the thrill of the search remains important for many consumers, some are put off by the hassle and fear of landing a counterfeit. Here, platforms need to offer smoother shopping processes to unlock a larger portion of the market.

Sources indicate that “Many shoppers still lack the confidence to complete a purchase because they are unsure whether they can trust the seller, the listing, or the protections available,” notes Keoghan, encouraging shoppers to use Ebay’s authenticity and money-back guarantees where necessary. That way, “they can be absolutely certain that the gift they’ve picked out is going to be right,” she says.

This matters. In the gifting economy, platforms are competing with more traditional dealers, many of whom have longstanding relationships with their clients. The key criteria for discerning gift shoppers? “Condition is always my first consideration. I want a piece to be beautifully preserved, especially when I’m buying it as a gift,” says Li. “Beyond that, I really appreciate sellers who understand the history of their objects,” noting the importance of when something was made, how it was used, and what makes it interesting. Li is also hot on transparency, especially regarding authenticity and restorations that might have taken place on a given item. “I value dealers who are knowledgeable, honest, and genuinely passionate about what they sell,” she says.

In this vein, The RealReal offers a filtering function to streamline products that are “pristine” (new with tags), and the platform curates holiday gifting edits online and in-store that are informed by the brands, categories and pieces customers are most interested in by location. Additionally, the platform’s retail experts can offer personalized guidance for clients finding a gift based on the recipient’s taste, lifestyle and wardrobe.

“HNWIs are used to high-touch clienteling, discretion and access, so they expect private sourcing, authentication and care that feels closer to a luxury store than a resale feed,” says Sophy Vanner Critoph, strategy partner at creative agency Amplify. “Aspirational shoppers want speed, sharp cultural curation and zero friction: clear grading, fast delivery and a seamless experience that feels current and reliable.”.

Resee’s inventory constantly shifts, but the focus remains on provenance and historical value.

Recent findings suggest that another issue for platforms to address? Shoppers with less fashion knowledge might be scared to buy something secondhand; the primary market has already been vouched for by a department store or a sales advisor. And if the gift isn’t right, vintage often involves more convoluted return processes, compared to the streamlined approach of online primary retail.

“We kept hearing women who would say, ‘I don’t want my husband to pick anything out for me. I just want him to give me something so I can buy myself something on Reiss,” states Bernardin. “So, we decided to do a vintage gift card.” Women’s History Museum Vintage also offers gift cards if the gift-giver isn’t confident in picking themselves. “There’s always an option to give the gift of a [vintage] shopping gift,” confirms Barringer. “In person, at our shop, via our website, or even Instagram.”.

Tech Report: Naomi Watts and Maude’s Éva Goicochea on Modernizing Sexual Wellness

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that naomi Watts founded her brand, Stripes Beauty, after starting menopause at 36.
  • Sources indicate that at the Vogue Business Global Summit: New York, Watts and Goicochea sat down to discuss their experiences in creating brands for themselves first, what progress has been made in opening up access to women’s sexual health, and why getting older doesn’t mean that women should have to give up on their sex lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s 2026, and women’s sex drives are still taboo. A crop of modern brands want to change that, with better products, more education and packaging you want sitting on your bedside table.

Sources indicate that naomi Watts founded her brand, Stripes Beauty, after starting menopause at 36. She found her typical products no longer worked, and that she didn’t understand how to navigate this stage of life — unexpectedly early — because she never had conversations about it with her mother. Maude founder Éva Goicochea started her brand with a vision to bring more access and smarter design to products once relegated to hush-hush purchasing.

Sources indicate that at the Vogue Business Global Summit: New York, Watts and Goicochea sat down to discuss their experiences in creating brands for themselves first, what progress has been made in opening up access to women’s sexual health, and why getting older doesn’t mean that women should have to give up on their sex lives. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

According to recent reports, vogue: We’re here to talk about women’s sexual health. How did you both end up in this space?

Industry observers note that naomi Watts: I stumbled into menopause much earlier than I was prepared for. I was trying to get pregnant, and I didn’t understand why I was failing at that, and my doctor did some blood work and told me that I was close to menopause. I was 36 years old, guys. So, it filled me with panic. After that, I realized I had had so many symptoms in the lead-up to that that were just sort of brushed off as nothing. I had night sweats, I had thinning periods, I had periods that were close together. And there was no information. I called my mom and said, ‘Why didn’t you tell me more about this?’ and she said, ‘These were the conversations I never had with you because my mother never had them with me.’ And so it was this cone of silence that was just agreed upon, that women must zip it and suffer in silence.

Sources indicate that so it took me about 10 years to get organized, but at 45, I started thinking about this product line. I was insistent at the beginning of our launch that we have two products, which are vaginal moisturizer and lube. I needed it myself, and I figured some others out there would, too.

Éva Goicochea: My mom did the opposite; she handed me Our Bodies, Ourselves when I was 5. And I was like, ‘OK’. But I’m from Newly introduced Mexico, and it’s a state that really has very poor sex education. So, I was always hyper-aware. I became a legislative aide in healthcare, but I always had a heart for design. And at some point, I had that lightbulb moment, and it was: use design to destigmatize, and use design to create awareness. And that is what I did. So, I left LA, where I was living, and I moved here to start Maude, and the idea was to use design and inclusivity to break barriers. And that’s where we are.

Naomi Watts and Éva Goicochea on stage at the Vogue Business Global Summit: Upcoming York.

Vogue: Why do you think that these taboos have existed in the first place?

Recent findings suggest that ÉG: It’s not that we don’t understand — maybe in some households or in some partnerships — that it’s OK to talk about this. I think we’ve just been told via product and the aisle and politics and policy that it’s not OK.

Sources indicate that NW: I think that’s beautifully noted, and I would agree with that. Women specifically have always had these health gaps and education gaps, and have been taught not to complain too much and just grin and bear it. And so much of sexuality, I think, is wrapped up in youth, and sex has been about reproductive stuff. As a woman ages, she becomes more sure of herself and more intentional about how she wants to put herself out there, be it in conversation, in the sack, whatever. I personally feel like there came a time when my hormones were not driving decisions, and I was able to authentically connect with my truth of what I felt like I wanted to do and what I didn’t. And when you get more organized with products, you don’t have to be uncomfortable. We can ride through the discomfort.

In a recent development, vogue: There’s a white space because, to your point, as women get older, attention can shift away. Do you think that we’re in a more progressive place when it comes to this?

ÉG: I do. I think it is changing, despite that sometimes it feels like we’re taking a few steps back. I do think there’s a lot of progress being made. Future generations are not putting up with this.

Sources indicate that NW: There are obviously pluses and minuses about social media, and you need to trust the sources, but we can generate information rapidly. I mean, certainly for me, it helped me find a community, because the only way to create change is through the power and the strength of other voices. I do think there’s still more progress to be made, and that certainly in my industry, I want to see [more complex] women reflected on the screen. We can run households, we can raise children, we can take care of the in-laws and the parents, we can run businesses, we can do all of these things and also deal with a hormonal, massive change. So let’s see that reflected on TV and movie screens as well.

According to recent reports, vogue: When it comes to menopause, what brands are out there that women can turn to? What was on the market when you started your companies?

NW: Because of the loss of estrogen, suddenly all these products I’d used before were not working. So I started looking, but I didn’t like this promise that you could reverse time and look 25 again. Sure, that would be great, but it’s not going to happen. I felt like there was nothing out there that was speaking the truth. I wanted to create a brand that could deal with all of these issues, and our tagline is ‘from scalp to vag’, because each point is a pain point for hydration. It’s about just really good ingredients for certain sensitivities, and we have identified what that woman’s needs are, because I am her.

It has been revealed that naomi Watts, who founded Stripes after starting menopause at 36. "I am her," she states of her customer.

It has been revealed that vogue: Éva, who is the Maude customer? Who did you want your products to speak to?

ÉG: Everyone over 18. And I was told that can’t be done, but I really think that inclusivity is such a key piece because we’ve probably all felt very excluded from this category. It’s always been gendered, it’s been ageist, we’ve been talked at, there are rarely women executives at the table. So with Maude, it was this idea of, if we’re not seeing it, let’s go make it happen.

Vogue: I want to get your take on younger customers in this space, because we hear a lot that Gen Z is not having sex, they’re not going out. But on the runways, sex is coming back into the fashion zeitgeist. How are you reading this moment when it comes to sex itself? Is it taboo? Are we talking about it? Are we having it?

ÉG: I was just thinking about this yesterday — I understand Y2K fashion is back, but I think Gen Z is wise enough to know not to bring back the culture of that time. It was really a hard time for women. That said, I also think Gen Z is very pressured to always have technology in the middle of their relationships. That’s how they’re supposed to find people. And a lot of them live at home, so I don’t blame them for not having sex. But I don’t think that’s because they don’t want to; I think they’re more empowered, more educated, more aware of what they want more than ever. So, I see it as an amazing signal that this generation, again, is not going to put up with what we put up with.

It has been revealed that vogue: Maude recently made a big retail push, which signifies an expansion or acceptance of this category. What were those conversations like with retailers?

ÉG: Target Beauty Studio and Ulta came to us at the same time. Target has an audience that is couples, people in their 30s, 40s, and beyond. We’re still represented in Target Beauty Studio only as a body brand, so we’re trying to get them to think a bit differently. And then Ulta has been much more open, because intimate wellness is one of their four pillars of wellness, so we do not have to explain ourselves. And they carry some of our sexual wellness products versus just body care. But they came to us. How we navigate that and the future with them, I think, will be a bit at a different pace, but they both seem very receptive.

Products from Maude, which founder Éva Goicochea started with one idea: "use design to destigmatize." The range sits body wash next to lube.

Vogue: Naomi, how is Stripes thinking about product expansion after launching with only two sexual health products?

NW: We’ve just recently debuted a gummy called Rite of Passion, and it’s backed by doctors. We developed it with Dr Cindy Meston and Dr Somi Javaid, and that was really crucial to me. It’s for sexual arousal, and we just launched it at Ulta, and we’re super excited. We really did it because we listened to our women, and the social listening told us that women feel like they don’t have sex in their marriages anymore, and sometimes it’s about drive, or sometimes it’s about pain. And there are things we can do for that, whether that’s lube, or estrogen, or more education. There’s no shame in it. You just need a little bit more mojo. I feel like I’m on this journey with them. The good news is that there’s really no more secrecy, there’s no more stigma, and women will readily open the conversation.

Rite of Passion, Stripes’s first product beyond its original lube and vaginal moisturiser, recently released at Ulta.

Vogue: As a celebrity founder, how do you feel you’re setting Stripes up for success from here and for the long term?

NW: It was born out of my need, but hopefully we’ve done a good job of being authentic and inclusive, and reflecting this woman, who she is and what her needs are. So it really should be able to live with or without me. That said, I don’t blueprint on going anywhere. Women come up to me, and instead of a selfie, they want to tell me about how they had a great conversation with their husbands, with their wives, with their children, with their boss, because permission was given to them that the dialogue was opened, and if I’ve had any part in that, I just feel so proud. It’s become my upcoming purpose.

Vogue: What’s the biggest thing you've learned as a founder so far?

Industry observers note that NW: Gosh. Just to continue to be authentic and to not be afraid of failure, and go after what you believe in. I’m someone who’s experienced a lot of failure as an actor, and had extreme highs, and some ones that just landed with a thud. I’m pretty thick-skinned. It’s not failure. It’s a fresh type of lesson that opens a door you may not have known existed.

ÉG: I live by the mantra that there is no arrival sign. I speak to a lot of founders, and they ask, ‘When am I going to wake up and feel like I’m accomplished?’ And I’m like, ‘You might not.’ And on having incredibly thick skin, it’s really not personal. You are the shepherd of your brand; it’s not about you, and that’s actually the most powerful thing you can do is recognize: ‘I have a responsibility to my customers or to my team or to the world.’ So that’s where I try to at least think for myself. ‘It’s not about you.’.

Vogue: What’s one thing that you both wish the rest of the industry would learn from women in this space, women founders? And what would you challenge the industry to do differently next year and beyond?

ÉG: I am so grateful to be in rooms that talk about beauty and wellness, but I want us all to pause and remember that sexual wellness is a human need. I want the reverence and respect to be there for this category, because it permeates every part of our lives. And it’s so crucial that we create gender parity in these conversations for our daughters. And I just want this to be seen as something that is so deeply, ornately part of us that we don’t think of it as a blip, as a trend. This is not a trend.

In a recent development, NW: For a woman who’s experiencing perimenopause and menopause, she should feel supported at every stage, and she should feel vibrant. And sexuality is something that a lot of great things can come out of. I’m lucky, I have a lovely new husband — we’ve only been married a couple of years. A woman shouldn’t feel like it’s all over. I love that positive message and just want to keep expanding that, and sex ed. We don’t learn about it. Menopause is not an end, it’s just a new chapter. Just because the hormones come to an end doesn’t mean your sex life has to.

Recent findings suggest that every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Recent findings suggest that to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

In a recent development, to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

It has been revealed that place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

According to recent reports, the secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

In a recent development, mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

In a recent development, lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Recent findings suggest that toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too swiftly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Industry observers note that last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • It has been revealed that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Industry observers note that last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

It has been revealed that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Recent findings suggest that which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Industry observers note that tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a newly introduced congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

In a recent development, run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a upcoming congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a newly introduced congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

It has been revealed that guv revision: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

Recent findings suggest that #TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

It has been revealed that senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

Recent findings suggest that AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Upcoming Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

In a recent development, ducking the wave: Democrats notched major wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Recent findings suggest that here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

According to recent reports, how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Fresh York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

In a recent development, if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Industry observers note that vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

Recent findings suggest that welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing blueprint you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

Sources indicate that in other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a latest study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

Sources indicate that at Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

Industry observers note that the gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the manufacturer imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its significant flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

Industry observers note that I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

In a recent development, semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a upcoming study published in the New England Journal of Medicine indicates that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, intends to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the rapidly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

In a recent development, as a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

In a recent development, at Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.
